claims.claim: Adult songbirds can adaptively modify specific elements of their song structure in response to somatosensory feedback.
claims.source: We first tested whether adult songbirds can adaptively modify specific elements of their song structure in response to somatosensory feedback (Figure 1b, Experiment 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and referenced in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: Mild cutaneous electrical stimulation was used as non-auditory stimuli delivered during ongoing song performance.
claims.source: We used non-auditory stimuli (mild cutaneous electrical stimulation), which we delivered during ongoing song performance, to differentially reinforce the acoustics (fundamental frequency, or 'pitch') of specific song elements, or 'syllables.'
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: Brief playbacks of white noise are a well-established paradigm for driving changes in pitch in adult songbirds.
claims.source: In separate experiments, we tested birds using auditory stimuli consisting of brief playbacks of white noise, a well-established paradigm for driving changes in pitch in adult songbirds (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Tumer and Brainard, 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Tumer and Brainard, 2007.

claims.claim: LMAN is the output nucleus of the AFP.
claims.source: We next assessed the neural circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory-driven vocal learning by determining the necessity of LMAN (the output nucleus of the AFP) for somatosensory learning (Figure 1b, Experiment 2).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the songbird brain.

claims.claim: LMAN is necessary for somatosensory vocal learning.
claims.source: We next assessed the neural circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory-driven vocal learning by determining the necessity of LMAN (the output nucleus of the AFP) for somatosensory learning (Figure 1b, Experiment 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by lesion experiments.

claims.claim: Dopaminergic input to Area X is necessary for non-auditory vocal learning.
claims.source: Finally, we assessed the role of dopaminergic neural circuitry in somatosensory vocal learning by performing selective lesions of dopaminergic input to Area X (Figure 1b, Experiment 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by lesion experiments.

claims.claim: Songbirds naturally produce many renditions of song every day, which consist of repeated patterns of unique vocal gestures called syllables.
claims.source: Every day, songbirds naturally produce many renditions of song, which consist of repeated patterns of unique vocal gestures, called syllables (Figure 2b, top).
claims.evidence: This describes natural songbird behavior, supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: There is rendition-to-rendition variability in the fundamental frequency (pitch) of song syllables.
claims.source: For one 'target' syllable in each experimental subject, we quantified rendition-to-rendition variability in the fundamental frequency (which we refer to here as 'pitch') of each occurrence of this syllable on the final baseline day (Figure 2b, top).
claims.evidence: This describes an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Cutaneous stimulation was triggered in real time (within 40 ms of syllable onset) when the pitch of the target syllable fell within a specified range.
claims.source: To differentially reinforce the pitch of a target syllable, we determined a range of pitches within this baseline distribution (either all pitches above the 20th percentile or all pitches below the 80th percentile), and then triggered the delivery of cutaneous stimulation in real time (within 40 ms of syllable onset) when the pitch of the target syllable fell within this range (Figure 2b, bottom).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: Birds could choose not to sing in order to avoid triggering cutaneous stimulation.
claims.source: Note that the birds could choose not to sing in order to avoid triggering any cutaneous stimulation, and we carefully monitored animal subjects for any signs of distress (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This describes an aspect of the experimental design and animal welfare monitoring.

claims.claim: In the example experiment, the bird gradually changed the pitch of the targeted syllable downward (the adaptive direction), such that cutaneous stimulation was triggered less frequently.
claims.source: In this example experiment, the bird gradually changed the pitch of the targeted syllable downward (the adaptive direction), such that cutaneous stimulation was triggered less frequently (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This describes the results from an example experiment shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: In the example experiment, at the start of the first day of cutaneous stimulation training, 80% of syllable renditions resulted in cutaneous stimulation and 20% resulted in escapes.
claims.source: In the example experiment, at the start of the first day of cutaneous stimulation training, 80% of syllable renditions resulted in cutaneous stimulation and 20% of syllable renditions resulted in escapes.
claims.evidence: This describes quantitative results from the example experiment.

claims.claim: On the third (final) day of cutaneous stimulation training in the example experiment, escapes occurred on over 60% of target syllable renditions.
claims.source: On the third (final) day of cutaneous stimulation training, escapes occurred on over 60% of target syllable renditions and the entire distribution of pitches had changed significantly in the adaptive direction, indicating that a significant amount of vocal learning occurred in this example experiment (Figure 2d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to assess the difference between baseline and end of cutaneous stimulation training, p=1.1776e-12).
claims.evidence: This describes quantitative results from the example experiment shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: The entire distribution of pitches changed significantly in the adaptive direction by the end of cutaneous stimulation training in the example experiment (p=1.1776e-12).
claims.source: On the third (final) day of cutaneous stimulation training, escapes occurred on over 60% of target syllable renditions and the entire distribution of pitches had changed significantly in the adaptive direction, indicating that a significant amount of vocal learning occurred in this example experiment (Figure 2d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to assess the difference between baseline and end of cutaneous stimulation training, p=1.1776e-12).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the example experiment, shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: After 6 days of washout, there was no significant difference between the distribution of target syllable pitches at the end of washout compared to baseline (p=0.606) in the example experiment.
claims.source: After 6 days of washout, there was no significant difference between the distribution of target syllable pitches at the end of washout compared to baseline (Figure 2d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.606).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the example experiment, shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: Semitones provide a normalized measure of pitch change such that a one semitone change corresponds to a roughly 6% change in the absolute frequency of an acoustic signal.
claims.source: Semitones provide a normalized measure of pitch change such that a one semitone change corresponds to a roughly 6% change in the absolute frequency of an acoustic signal (see Equation 1).
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the measurement unit used in the study.

claims.claim: The mean pitch (in semitones) of the target syllables showed a significant, adaptive change from baseline on days 2 and 3 of cutaneous stimulation training (Pboot < 0.0010, n = 13 experiments in 12 birds).
claims.source: We found that the mean pitch (in semitones) of the target syllables showed a significant, adaptive change from baseline on days 2 and 3 of cutaneous stimulation training (Figure 2e; the probability of resampled mean pitch on cutaneous stimulation training days 2 and 3 lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, limit due to resampling 104 times, n = 13 experiments in 12 birds, one bird underwent two cutaneous stimulation experiments; Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary statistical finding from the study, shown in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Non-auditory feedback is sufficient to drive vocal learning in adult songbirds.
claims.source: This demonstrates that non-auditory feedback is sufficient to drive vocal learning in adult songbirds.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing adaptive pitch changes in response to cutaneous stimulation.

claims.claim: In all individual experiments where an upward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (upward) direction.
claims.source: In all individual experiments where an upward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (upward) direction, and in all experiments where a downwards pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (downward) direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This describes consistent results across all experiments, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: In all experiments where a downward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (downward) direction.
claims.source: In all individual experiments where an upward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (upward) direction, and in all experiments where a downwards pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (downward) direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This describes consistent results across all experiments, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: The order of white noise training and cutaneous stimulation training was randomized for birds that underwent both training paradigms.
claims.source: To account for the potential influence of multiple trainings in the same individual birds on magnitude of learning, we randomized the order of white noise training and cutaneous stimulation training for the birds that underwent both training paradigms.
claims.evidence: This describes an aspect of the experimental design to control for order effects.

claims.claim: There was no statistically significant difference between the magnitude of learning by the end of training in birds that did not undergo craniotomies compared with birds that received sham LMAN lesions for either white noise experiments (p=0.779) or cutaneous stimulation experiments (p=0.148).
claims.source: Also, we found no statistically significant difference between the magnitude of learning by the end of training in birds that did not undergo craniotomies for LMAN, 6-OHDA, or sham lesions compared with the magnitude of learning in birds that received sham LMAN lesions for either white noise experiments (two-sample t-test, p=0.779) or cutaneous stimulation experiments (two-sample t-test, p=0.148).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing learning magnitudes across experimental groups.

claims.claim: By the end of white noise training, the adaptive pitch change (in semitones) across all white noise experiments performed in unoperated birds was significantly greater than baseline (Pboot < 0.0010).
claims.source: Consistent with prior studies (Ali et al., 2013; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Tumer and Brainard, 2007), by the end of white noise training, the adaptive pitch change (in semitones) across all white noise experiments performed in unoperated birds (birds that had wire electrodes surgically implanted but received no invasive brain procedures like sham operations) was significantly greater than baseline (zero) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a; the probability of resampled mean pitch on all three cutaneous stimulation training days lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010; Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result consistent with prior studies, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claims.claim: In birds that underwent sham operations, significant adaptive pitch changes were observed in response to white noise bursts (Pboot < 0.0010).
claims.source: In the separate experimental group of birds that underwent sham operations, we also observed significant adaptive pitch changes in response to white noise bursts, as expected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b; the probability of resampled mean pitch on all three cutaneous stimulation training days lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010; Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sham-operated birds, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claims.claim: There was no systematic difference between learning magnitude during cutaneous stimulation training and learning magnitude during white noise training (p=0.313).
claims.source: We found no systematic differences between learning magnitude during cutaneous stimulation training and the learning magnitude during white noise training (Figure 2f; paired t-test, p=0.313).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing learning magnitudes between two types of training, shown in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: Non-auditory stimuli can drive vocal learning as effectively as auditory stimuli.
claims.source: These results suggest that non-auditory stimuli can drive vocal learning as effectively as auditory stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of learning magnitudes between cutaneous stimulation and white noise training.

claims.claim: The normalized catch trials did not differ significantly from 1 in every experiment (0.071 < p < 0.997), indicating that the pitch of catch trials was highly similar to trials where cutaneous stimulation was provided.
claims.source: In every case, the normalized catch trials did not differ significantly from 1, indicating that the pitch of catch trials was highly similar to trials where cutaneous stimulation was provided (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a; t-test, 0.071 < p < 0.997 for each experiment; Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from catch trial analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between randomly selected baseline trials and normalized catch trials (p=0.339).
claims.source: There was no significant difference between this dataset and the normalized catch trials (paired t-test, p=0.339).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing catch trials to baseline trials.

claims.claim: The cutaneous stimulation on the scalp did not drive learning through an unexpected influence on brain activity in dorsal auditory areas of the pallium.
claims.source: To ensure that the cutaneous stimulation on the scalp did not drive learning through an unexpected influence on brain activity in dorsal auditory areas of the pallium, we implanted the wire electrodes in the neck instead of the scalp in 7 out of 12 birds used in these experiments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment comparing scalp and neck electrode placements.

claims.claim: The magnitude of vocal learning did not differ between birds with scalp electrodes and birds with neck electrodes on any day of training (0.679 < Pboot < 0.891).
claims.source: The magnitude of vocal learning did not differ between the two groups of birds on any day of training (0.679 < Pboot < 0.891).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing learning magnitudes between electrode placement groups.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the magnitude of learning between song collected between 10 AM and noon and song collected between 6 PM and 8 PM on any day of training (0.167 < Pboot < 0.951).
claims.source: Also, we reanalyzed this dataset by measuring syllable pitch from syllables produced in the evening (6 PM to 8 PM) instead of in the morning, and we found no significant difference in the magnitude of learning between song collected between 10 AM and noon and song collected between 6 PM and 8 PM on any day of training (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, 0.167 < Pboot < 0.951 on all days of training; Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from reanalysis of the data at different times of day, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: The gradual, adaptive pitch shift is driven by non-auditory cutaneous stimulation and not by other unintentional effects of the stimulation, the methodology of wire implantation, or the time window of song analysis.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that the gradual, adaptive pitch shift is driven by non-auditory cutaneous stimulation and not by other unintentional effects of the stimulation, the methodology of wire implantation, or the time window of song analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple control analyses ruling out alternative explanations.

claims.claim: LMAN lesions induced a significant reduction in pitch CV (p=0.002), while sham operations did not (p=0.911).
claims.source: LMAN lesions induced a significant reduction in pitch CV, sham operations did not (paired t-tests, p=0.002, p=0.911, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the LMAN lesion experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Prelesion learning magnitude during cutaneous stimulation training was significantly greater than baseline (Pboot < 0.0010).
claims.source: Prelesion, songbirds adaptively changed the pitch of the target syllable away from baseline in response to non-auditory feedback (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each day of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from prelesion experiments, shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: Postlesion, non-auditory vocal learning was abolished in LMAN-lesioned birds (0.297 < Pboot < 0.660 on the final 4 days of training, n = 6 birds).
claims.source: Postlesion, non-auditory vocal learning was abolished in those same birds (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each of the final 4 days of training lesser than or equal to zero was 0.297 < Pboot < 0.660, where 0.025 < Pboot < 0.975 indicates no significant difference, n = 6 birds; one bird from this group did not undergo prelesion experimentation) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from postlesion experiments, shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion in LMAN-lesioned birds (Pboot < 0.007 on each of the final 4 days of training).
claims.source: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion (Pboot < 0.007 on each of the final 4 days of training).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postlesion learning magnitudes.

claims.claim: Significant learning during cutaneous stimulation training was observed in both pre- and postsham-lesioned datasets (Pboot < 0.0010, n = 5 birds).
claims.source: We observed significant learning during cutaneous stimulation training in both pre- and postsham-lesioned datasets (Figure 3e, for both presham and postsham datasets, the probability of resampled mean pitch on each day of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, n = 5 birds; Figure 3—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sham-lesioned experiments, shown in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: The learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ in pre- vs. postsham datasets (0.120 < Pboot < 0.524).
claims.source: Also, the learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ in pre- vs. postsham datasets (the probability of resampled mean pitch of presham data on each day of training lesser than or equal to resampled mean pitch of postlesion data was 0.120 < Pboot < 0.524).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postsham learning magnitudes.

claims.claim: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds was significantly greater than that for sham-operated birds at the end of fixed threshold training (p=0.036, n = 5 birds in both groups).
claims.source: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds was significantly greater than that for sham-operated birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.036, n = 5 birds in both groups).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lesion effects between groups, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds at the end of staircase training was significantly greater than for sham-lesioned birds (p=0.004, n = 5 birds in both groups).
claims.source: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds calculated at this time point was also significantly greater than for sham-lesioned birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.004, n = 5 birds in both groups).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lesion effects between groups, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: LMAN is required for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds.
claims.source: These results show that LMAN is required for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds, indicating that both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback engage the AFP to drive adaptive changes to song.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LMAN lesion experiments showing abolished learning postlesion.

claims.claim: Both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback engage the AFP to drive adaptive changes to song.
claims.source: These results show that LMAN is required for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds, indicating that both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback engage the AFP to drive adaptive changes to song.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that LMAN is required for both auditory and non-auditory vocal learning.

claims.claim: Selective lesions of dopaminergic projections in Area X were performed via bilateral 6-OHDA injections.
claims.source: Selective lesions of dopaminergic projections in Area X were performed via bilateral 6-OHDA injections in Area X (see 'Materials and methods'), and the effectiveness of the 6-OHDA injections at lesioning dopaminergic innervation in Area X was quantified (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for dopamine lesions.

claims.claim: 6-OHDA injections selectively lesion dopaminergic inputs to Area X without damaging non-dopaminergic cells.
claims.source: This approach has previously been shown to selectively lesion dopaminergic inputs to Area X without damaging non-dopaminergic cells (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Saravanan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Saravanan et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Neither dopamine lesions nor sham operations induced significant changes in pitch CV (p=0.397 and p=0.531, respectively).
claims.source: Dopaminergic lesions in Area X did not induce a significant change in syllable CV (Figure 4b; paired t-test, p=0.397; Figure 4—source data 1). Sham operations also did not induce a significant change in syllable CV (Figure 4b; paired t-test, p=0.531).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the dopamine lesion experiments, shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The lesion-induced changes in syllable CV (post – pre) were not significantly different for 6-OHDA-lesioned birds than for sham-lesioned birds (p=0.054).
claims.source: The lesion-induced changes in syllable CV (post – pre) were not significantly different for 6-OHDA-lesioned birds than for sham-lesioned birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.054).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lesion effects on CV between groups, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: The dopamine lesion methodology used spares about 50% of the dopaminergic input to Area X.
claims.source: It is likely that the dopamine lesion methodology we used, which spares about 50% of the dopaminergic input to Area X Hoffmann et al., 2016, is insufficient to impair dopamine-mediated generation of syllable variability.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Prelesion, songbirds adaptively changed the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (Pboot < 0.010 on the final 4 days).
claims.source: Prelesion, songbirds adaptively changed the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each of the final 4 days of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.010) (Figure 4c, Figure 4—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from prelesion experiments, shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: Postlesion, 6-OHDA-lesioned birds were not able to adaptively change the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (0.067 < Pboot < 0.553 on the first 4 days; Pboot < 0.0010 on the final day, n = 5 birds).
claims.source: Postlesion, these same birds were not able to adaptively change the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each of the first 4 days of training lesser than or equal to zero was 0.067 < Pboot < 0.553; the probability of resampled mean pitch on the final day of training greater than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, n = 5 birds).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from postlesion experiments.

claims.claim: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion in 6-OHDA-lesioned birds (Pboot < 0.0010 on the final 3 days of training).
claims.source: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion (the probability of resampled mean pitch from prelesion dataset on each of the final 3 days of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to resampled mean pitch from postlesion dataset was Pboot < 0.0010).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postlesion learning magnitudes.

claims.claim: Both pre- and postsham, songbirds displayed significant amounts of learning during cutaneous stimulation training (Pboot < 0.0010, n = 3 birds).
claims.source: Both pre- and postsham, songbirds displayed significant amounts of learning during cutaneous stimulation training (Figure 4d; the probability of resampled mean pitch from the presham dataset on each day other than day 2 of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010; the probability of resampled mean pitch from the postsham dataset on each day of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, n = 3 birds; Figure 4—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from sham-lesioned experiments, shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: The learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ pre- vs. postsham in dopamine lesion experiments (0.653 < Pboot < 0.931).
claims.source: Also, the learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ pre- vs. postsham (the probability of resampled mean pitch of presham data on each day of training lesser than or equal to resampled mean pitch of postlesion data was 0.653 < Pboot < 0.931).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postsham learning magnitudes.

claims.claim: Dopaminergic input to Area X is required for adaptive changes in vocal output in response to non-auditory signals.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that dopaminergic input to Area X is required for adaptive changes in vocal output in response to non-auditory signals.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dopamine lesion experiments showing abolished learning postlesion.

claims.claim: Adult vocal learning is not solely dependent on auditory feedback.
claims.source: These results show that adult vocal learning is not solely dependent on auditory feedback, and that the songbird AFP is not specialized just for processing auditory feedback for vocal learning, as has previously been hypothesized (Murdoch et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that non-auditory feedback can drive vocal learning.

claims.claim: The songbird AFP is not specialized just for processing auditory feedback for vocal learning.
claims.source: These results show that adult vocal learning is not solely dependent on auditory feedback, and that the songbird AFP is not specialized just for processing auditory feedback for vocal learning, as has previously been hypothesized (Murdoch et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that the AFP is required for non-auditory vocal learning, contradicting a previous hypothesis.

claims.claim: The AFP processes auditory feedback as well as non-auditory feedback to drive vocal learning.
claims.source: Instead, these results, in conjunction with prior work using visual cues to drive changes in vocal output (Zai et al., 2020), indicate that the AFP processes auditory feedback as well as non-auditory feedback to drive vocal learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and prior work on visual cues.

claims.claim: The AFP processes somatosensory information to guide vocal learning.
claims.source: Our results further show that the AFP processes somatosensory information to guide vocal learning, and that dopaminergic neural circuitry is necessary for non-auditory learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Dopaminergic neural circuitry is necessary for non-auditory learning.
claims.source: Our results further show that the AFP processes somatosensory information to guide vocal learning, and that dopaminergic neural circuitry is necessary for non-auditory learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dopamine lesion experiments.

claims.claim: Songbird vocal muscles use somatosensory feedback to compensate for experimentally induced changes in respiratory pressure during song performance.
claims.source: Prior work has shown that songbird vocal muscles use somatosensory feedback to compensate for experimentally induced changes in respiratory pressure during song performance (Suthers et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Suthers et al., 2002.

claims.claim: The AFP could play a role in processing somatosensory information from vocal muscles to guide song performance.
claims.source: The result that the AFP underlies vocal learning driven by somatosensory signals (cutaneous stimulation) suggests that it could play a role in processing somatosensory information from vocal muscles to guide song performance.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of the AFP based on the current findings.

claims.claim: The AFP can integrate sensory information from a wide variety of sources of sensory feedback, even those not directly produced by vocalizations.
claims.source: Also, the fact that mild cutaneous stimulation is different than the direct proprioceptive feedback from vocal muscles or vocal effectors, yet the AFP still underlies vocal learning in response to cutaneous stimulation, suggests that the AFP can integrate sensory information from a wide variety of sources of sensory feedback, even those not directly produced by vocalizations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that the AFP processes cutaneous stimulation, which is not directly related to vocal production.

claims.claim: Songbird ventral pallidum (VP) receives input from auditory cortical areas, encodes auditory feedback information, and projects to VTA.
claims.source: For example, recent work has demonstrated that songbird ventral pallidum (VP) receives input from auditory cortical areas, encodes auditory feedback information, and projects to VTA (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The VP-VTA pathway represents a likely pathway by which sensory information from white noise bursts could influence neural activity in VTA, which could then drive changes in the AFP that promote song learning.
claims.source: This represents a likely pathway by which sensory information from white noise bursts could influence neural activity in VTA, which could then drive changes in the AFP that promote song learning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the neural pathway based on the cited work.

claims.claim: Comparatively less is known about the pathways in the songbird brain that might carry sensory information from cutaneous stimulation to the AFP.
claims.source: Comparatively less is known about the pathways in the songbird brain that might carry sensory information from cutaneous stimulation to the AFP.

results.result: Non-auditory somatosensory feedback (cutaneous electrical stimulation) can drive adaptive vocal learning in adult songbirds with similar effectiveness as auditory feedback. Birds adaptively changed syllable pitch in response to pitch-contingent cutaneous stimulation (Pboot < 0.0010 on days 2-3, n=13 experiments), with learning magnitudes comparable to white noise training (p=0.313). Multiple control analyses confirmed the learning was driven by cutaneous stimulation rather than artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C58 collectively demonstrate that cutaneous stimulation drives vocal learning through rigorous experimental design with appropriate controls. The statistical evidence is strong (Pboot < 0.0010), sample size is adequate (n=13 experiments in 12 birds), and multiple control experiments (catch trials, electrode placement, time-of-day analysis) rule out alternative explanations. The comparison to white noise training provides a validated benchmark.

results.result: LMAN, the output nucleus of the AFP, is necessary for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds. LMAN lesions abolished non-auditory vocal learning (postlesion: 0.297 < Pboot < 0.660, n=6 birds) while prelesion learning was significant (Pboot < 0.0010). Sham operations did not impair learning (Pboot < 0.0010 both pre- and postsham, n=5 birds). Lesion efficacy was confirmed by reduced pitch CV (p=0.002) and histological analysis (p<0.0010).
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C59-C68, C119-C122 provide strong evidence for LMAN's necessity through within-subject pre/post-lesion design with appropriate sham controls. The behavioral effect (abolished learning) is robust, lesion efficacy is confirmed through multiple methods (CV reduction, histology showing 80-100% lesion), and statistical evidence is compelling. The hierarchical bootstrap approach appropriately accounts for data structure.

results.result: Dopaminergic input to Area X is necessary for non-auditory vocal learning. 6-OHDA lesions of dopaminergic projections to Area X abolished adaptive learning (postlesion: 0.067 < Pboot < 0.553 on days 1-4, n=5 birds) while prelesion learning was significant (Pboot < 0.010). Sham operations preserved learning (Pboot < 0.0010 pre- and postsham, n=3 birds). Lesion efficacy was confirmed histologically (p<0.001), though lesions spared ~50% of dopaminergic input.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C69-C79, C84, C92-C93, C123-C125 demonstrate dopamine's necessity through pre/post-lesion design with sham controls. The statistical evidence is strong, histological confirmation validates lesion efficacy, and the lack of CV changes (C71-C72) confirms learning deficits aren't due to reduced variability. However, C92-C93 note an anti-adaptive change on day 5 that requires cautious interpretation due to experimental disruptions, slightly weakening but not invalidating the overall conclusion.

results.result: The AFP processes both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback to guide adaptive vocal changes, demonstrating it is not specialized solely for auditory feedback processing. Both LMAN and dopaminergic inputs to Area X are necessary for non-auditory vocal learning, indicating the AFP integrates multiple sensory modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C68, C80-C83 synthesize the experimental findings into a broader conclusion about AFP function. This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from Experiments 1-3 showing: (1) non-auditory feedback drives learning, (2) LMAN is necessary for this learning, and (3) dopaminergic inputs are necessary. The claim contradicts prior hypotheses (C81, citing Murdoch et al., 2018) based on solid experimental evidence.

results.result: Experimental design controls demonstrate that learning is not confounded by surgical procedures or training order. The order of white noise and cutaneous stimulation training was randomized, and there were no significant differences in learning magnitude between unoperated birds and sham-lesioned birds for either white noise (p=0.779) or cutaneous stimulation (p=0.148) experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 describe important methodological controls that strengthen the validity of the main findings. The randomization of training order (C47) controls for order effects, and the lack of differences between unoperated and sham-lesioned birds (C48) confirms that surgical procedures per se don't affect learning. These controls are appropriately implemented and statistically validated.

results.result: Methodological details of the experimental approach: Adult male Bengalese finches (>100 days old) were used, with all singing undirected. Cutaneous stimulation parameters were 50 ms duration, 100-350 μA current, delivered within 20-30 ms of syllable onset. Pitch changes were measured in semitones (1 semitone ≈ 6% frequency change). Birds could choose not to sing to avoid stimulation, and spontaneous pitch restoration occurred during washout.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C36, C42, C112-C118 provide essential methodological details that are clearly described and appropriate for the experimental goals. The stimulation parameters are justified (behaviorally salient but not distressing), the measurement units are standard, and the washout observations confirm reversibility. These details support reproducibility and proper interpretation of results.

results.result: The AFP may integrate diverse sensory information beyond direct vocal feedback and could play broader roles in vocal behavior. The AFP might process somatosensory information from vocal muscles, integrate sensory information from sources not directly produced by vocalizations, and be involved in processing non-auditory sensory information during social behaviors involving vocal communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C86-C87, C89-C91, C97 are speculative interpretations extending beyond the direct experimental evidence. While C55 is supported by the control experiment showing no difference between scalp and neck electrode placements, claims C86-C87, C89-C91, and C97 are reasonable hypotheses based on the findings but lack direct experimental validation. These represent promising directions for future research rather than established results.

results.result: The findings may reflect general principles for vocal plasticity across species and have implications for understanding human speech mechanisms. The AFP may encode general information about vocal performance outcomes ('good' vs 'bad') rather than solely auditory performance error. The analogous vocal circuitry in humans may also underlie non-auditory vocal learning and process multimodal sensory signals during speech.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C98-C111 discuss broader implications and comparisons to human speech. While the songbird-human analogies are well-established in the literature (C106), the specific extrapolations about AFP function (C105) and human speech mechanisms (C109-C111) are speculative. The discussion of whether white noise represents performance error vs. aversive stimulus (C99, C103) is thoughtful but unresolved. These represent important theoretical considerations but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: Background context and prior work: Songbirds and humans share vocal learning abilities and rely on auditory feedback throughout life. Prior research has focused primarily on auditory feedback, with recent work showing visual cues also shape vocalizations. The AFP is required for auditory-guided vocal learning, with LMAN lesions preventing auditory vocal plasticity and dopaminergic manipulations in Area X impairing learning. However, the role of non-auditory somatosensory feedback in vocal learning remained unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C26, C29-C30, C85, C88, C94-C96 accurately summarize established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims correctly identify the gap in knowledge (C3, C14, C25-C26) that motivates the current study. The characterization of prior work is accurate and well-supported by the cited references.
